steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on multi-armed bandit recommendation systems where the recommendations themselves change what users prefer, so the goal becomes shaping the population's preferences instead of just finding the best arm. Motivate the problem, describe our influence models, and end with the list of contributions and the paper outline.

- Problem with the classical assumption: recommendations influence preferences
- Our objective: shape preferences, not find the best arm (link to opinion control)
- Our setting: multitype population, positive/negative influence, two influence models
- Key contributions
- Organization of the paper

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- MAB algorithms and recommendation systems
  - stochastic MAB used in many applications; canonical one = recommendation systems (suggest items from fixed set)
  - examples: e-commerce, streaming, friends/connections on social networks, results and ads in search engines
  - classical setting: users arrive sequentially, recommended one of N arms; random reward from user preference
  - reward distributions independent, unknown
  - goal: learn best arm, minimize loss in cumulative reward vs ideal/reference algorithm, finite horizon
  - relevant extension: contextual bandits (side info on user preferences)
- Problem with the classical assumption
  - key assumption: reward distributions don't change with time -> preferences not affected by arms played
  - not true in practice: recommendations affect preferences; advertisements exist to persuade
  - our assumption: preferences (so reward distributions) depend on history of recommendations, function of arms played and rewards accrued
- Our objective
  - usual MAB: best arm (highest expected reward), exploration + exploitation
  - ours: actively use preference reinforcements to influence population preferences
  - similar in spirit to opinion control literature (cite); not explored in MAB setting
- Our setting
  - contextual MAB, multitype population, each type has unique preferred arm
  - positive influence (arm liked) and negative influence (not liked), simultaneously
  - (1) decreasing intensity of influence, population increasingly rigid — advertising gives diminishing returns (cite)
  - (2) constant intensity of influence — voter model (cite), opinion dynamics
  - first: two types, type 1 preferred; maximize type 1 population at end of horizon T
- Key contributions
  - optimal policy, known reward statistics; doesn't necessarily recommend favoured arm [Section IV]
  - ETC policy, unknown statistics; twin tradeoffs; logarithmic regret, known horizon [Section V]
  - Thompson sampling policy; logarithmic regret, unknown horizon [Section V]
  - constant influence model: analyses and algorithms stay valid [Section VI]
  - extensions: N-arm MAB for N-type population (optimal policy with known reward matrix, Thompson sampling) [VII-A]; two competing recommendation systems, two-arm two-type, preliminary [VII-B]
- Organization
  - Section II related literature; Section III model and preliminaries; conclusion with future work; proofs in appendix

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Stochastic multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms are used in a lot of applications. One canonical application is recommendation systems, which suggest one or more items out of a fixed set of items to the users of the system. These recommendation systems are used for example to suggest items on e-commerce websites and streaming services, to recommend friends and connections on social networks, and to place results and ads in search engines. In the classical stochastic MAB setting, users arrive one after another and each one is recommended one of N arms. The system gets a random reward that depends on the user preference for the arm that was recommended. The reward distribution of each arm is unknown and is assumed to be independent of all the other rewards. What the MAB algorithm wants is to learn the best arm while minimizing the loss in cumulative reward over a finite time horizon, where the loss is compared to the reward of an ideal or reference algorithm. There are many extensions of this classical problem, and the one that is relevant for our work is contextual bandits, where the algorithm also has side information about the preferences of the user.

Classical MAB algorithms are designed and analysed under the key assumption that the reward distributions of the arms do not change with time. This also means it is assumed that the preferences of the user population are not affected by the sequence of arms that are played. But from one's own experience this is clearly not always true, because user preferences are affected by the recommendations. Actually the whole objective of advertisements is to persuade users to adopt particular preferences. So in this paper we make the reasonable assumption that user preferences are not independent of the recommendations but are influenced by them. More specifically, we assume that the preferences of the users at any time, and so the reward distributions of the arms, depend on the history of recommendations up to that time, and are a function of the arms that were played and the rewards that were accrued.

Usually MAB algorithms are designed to find the best arm, meaning the one with the highest expected reward, by combining exploration and exploitation in a judicious way. Our objective is quite different from this. The goal here is to actively use the preference reinforcements in order to influence the preferences of the population. This objective is similar in spirit to the emerging literature on opinion control. However, as far as we know, this kind of objective has not been explored in an MAB setting.

- Our setting
  - contextual MAB, multitype population, each type has unique preferred arm
  - positive influence (arm liked) and negative influence (not liked), at the same time
  - two influence models: (1) decreasing intensity, population more rigid — advertising gives diminishing returns; (2) constant intensity — voter model, opinion dynamics
  - first two types, type 1 preferred; maximize type 1 users at end of horizon T
- Key contributions
  - optimal policy with known reward statistics; doesn't necessarily recommend favoured arm [Section IV]
  - ETC policy, unknown statistics; twin tradeoffs; logarithmic regret with known horizon [Section V]
  - Thompson sampling policy; logarithmic regret even with unknown horizon [Section V]
  - constant influence model: same analyses and algorithms valid [Section VI]
  - extensions: N-arm N-type (optimal policy, Thompson sampling) [Section VII-A]; two competing recommendation systems, preliminary [Section VII-B]
- Organization
  - related literature next; Section III model; conclusion with future work; proofs in appendix

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Stochastic multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms are used in a lot of applications. One canonical application is recommendation systems, which suggest one or more items out of a fixed set of items to the users of the system. These recommendation systems are used for example to suggest items on e-commerce websites and streaming services, to recommend friends and connections on social networks, and to place results and ads in search engines. In the classical stochastic MAB setting, users arrive one after another and each one is recommended one of N arms. The system gets a random reward that depends on the user preference for the arm that was recommended. The reward distribution of each arm is unknown and is assumed to be independent of all the other rewards. What the MAB algorithm wants is to learn the best arm while minimizing the loss in cumulative reward over a finite time horizon, where the loss is compared to the reward of an ideal or reference algorithm. There are many extensions of this classical problem, and the one that is relevant for our work is contextual bandits, where the algorithm also has side information about the preferences of the user.

Classical MAB algorithms are designed and analysed under the key assumption that the reward distributions of the arms do not change with time. This also means it is assumed that the preferences of the user population are not affected by the sequence of arms that are played. But from one's own experience this is clearly not always true, because user preferences are affected by the recommendations. Actually the whole objective of advertisements is to persuade users to adopt particular preferences. So in this paper we make the reasonable assumption that user preferences are not independent of the recommendations but are influenced by them. More specifically, we assume that the preferences of the users at any time, and so the reward distributions of the arms, depend on the history of recommendations up to that time, and are a function of the arms that were played and the rewards that were accrued.

Usually MAB algorithms are designed to find the best arm, meaning the one with the highest expected reward, by combining exploration and exploitation in a judicious way. Our objective is quite different from this. The goal here is to actively use the preference reinforcements in order to influence the preferences of the population. This objective is similar in spirit to the emerging literature on opinion control. However, as far as we know, this kind of objective has not been explored in an MAB setting.

In this paper we assume that the recommendation system uses a contextual MAB algorithm to serve a multitype population, where each type has a unique preferred arm. We allow positive and negative influences to be present at the same time. The influence is positive when the user likes the recommended arm and it is negative when the user does not like the recommendation. We also consider two kinds of time-dependent behavior of the influence dynamics. The first one is decreasing intensity of influence, where the population gets more and more rigid in its preferences, and the second one is constant intensity of influence, where the degree of influence stays constant during the whole period of interest. The first model is motivated by the empirical observation that advertising gives diminishing returns. The second model is inspired by the popular voter model (introduced in prior work), which has been widely studied in the opinion dynamics literature. For both models we first consider a system serving a population of two types, where type 1 is the preferred type, that is, the objective of the algorithm is to maximize the population of type 1 users at the end of the time horizon T.

The key contributions of the paper are the following.

- Optimal policy for maximizing the type 1 population when the reward statistics are known. The optimal policy does not necessarily recommend the favoured arm, which is interesting. [Section IV]

- An explore-then-commit (ETC) policy for maximizing the type 1 population when the reward statistics are unknown. This policy has to deal with two tradeoffs, the usual exploration-exploitation tradeoff and the decreasing ability to shape the preferences as the population gets more rigid. We also show it has logarithmic regret in the known time-horizon setting. [Section V]

- A policy based on Thompson sampling for maximizing the type 1 population when the reward statistics are unknown. We show this policy gives logarithmic regret even when the time-horizon is unknown. [Section V]

- For the constant influence model, we show that the analyses and algorithms we got for the decreasing influence model are still valid. [Section VI]

- Finally, we present two extensions. The first one is an N-arm MAB for an N-type population. For the objective of maximising the type 1 population we get the optimal policy when the reward matrix is known, and then we extend the Thompson sampling algorithm to this case. This is in Section VII-A. The second extension is a model for two recommendation systems that have competing objectives, for the two-arm, two-type case. Some preliminary results for this are in Section VII-B.

The related literature is discussed in the next section, where we also delineate our work. Section III sets up the model and some preliminaries. The paper concludes with a discussion of directions for future work. All the proofs are in the appendix.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Stochastic multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms are used in many applications. A canonical application is in recommendation systems that suggest one or more items from a fixed set of items to the users of the system. Examples of these recommendation systems are suggesting items on e-commerce websites and on streaming services, recommending friends and connections on social networks, and placing results and ads in search engines. The classical stochastic MAB setting is as follows. Users arrive sequentially and each is recommended one of N arms. The system obtains a random reward based on the user preference for the recommended arm. The reward distribution of each arm is assumed independent of all other rewards and is unknown. The objective of the MAB algorithm is to learn the best arm while minimizing the loss in cumulative reward, compared to that of an ideal or a reference algorithm, over a finite time horizon. Of the many extensions to this classical problem, the one relevant to our work is contextual bandits, where the algorithm also has side information about the user's preferences.

A key assumption in the design and analyses of classical MAB algorithms is that the reward distributions of the arms do not change with time. This also implies that the preferences of the user population are assumed not to be affected by the sequence of arms that are played. From one's own experience, the latter is clearly not always true—user preferences are affected by the recommendations. In fact, the objective of advertisements is to persuade users to adopt particular preferences. With this motivation, in this paper we make the reasonable assumption that user preferences are not independent of the recommendations and are in fact influenced by them. Specifically, we assume that the preferences of the users at any time, and hence the reward distributions of the arms, depend on the history of recommendations up to that time and are a function of the arms that are played and the rewards accrued.

MAB algorithms are usually designed to find the best arm, i.e., the one with the highest expected reward, by a judicious combination of exploration and exploitation. Our objective is a marked departure from this: the goal is to actively use the preference reinforcements to influence the population preferences. This objective is similar in spirit to the emerging literature on opinion control, e.g., [1,2,3]. However, to the best of our knowledge, such an objective has not been explored in an MAB setting.

In this paper, we assume that the recommendation system uses a contextual MAB algorithm to serve a multitype population, with each type having a unique preferred arm. We allow both positive and negative influences to be present simultaneously—influence is positive when the user likes the recommended arm and negative when the user does not like the recommendation. Furthermore, we consider two kinds of time-dependent behavior of the influence dynamics: (1) decreasing intensity of influence, where the population becomes increasingly rigid in its preferences, and (2) constant intensity of influence, where the degree of influence remains constant throughout the period of interest. The first model is motivated by the empirical observation that advertising gives diminishing returns [4], [5], and the second is inspired by the popular voter model (introduced in [6]), which has been widely studied in the opinion dynamics literature. For both models we first consider a system serving a population of two types with type 1 being the preferred type, i.e., the objective of the algorithm is to maximize the population of type 1 users at the end of the time horizon T.

The key contributions of the paper are the following.

- Optimal policy to maximize the type 1 population when the reward statistics are known. Interestingly, the optimal policy does not necessarily recommend the favoured arm. [Section IV]

- An explore-then-commit (ETC) policy to maximize the type 1 population when the reward statistics are unknown. This has to battle twin tradeoffs—the usual exploration-exploitation tradeoff and the decreasing ability to shape preferences as the population becomes more rigid. It is also shown to have logarithmic regret in the known time-horizon setting. [Section V]

- A Thompson sampling based policy to maximize the type 1 population when the reward statistics are unknown. We show that this policy gives logarithmic regret even if the time-horizon is unknown. [Section V]

- For the constant influence model, we show that the analyses and algorithms obtained for the decreasing influence model remain valid. [Section VI]

- Finally, we present two extensions. First, we describe an N-arm MAB for an N-type population. For the objective of maximising the type 1 population, we obtain the optimal policy when the reward matrix is known, and then extend the Thompson sampling algorithm to this case (Section VII-A). Second, we consider a model for two recommendation systems with competing objectives in the two-arm, two-type case, and present some preliminary results in Section VII-B.

In the next section we discuss the related literature and delineate our work. The model and some preliminaries are set up in Section III. We conclude the paper with a discussion of directions for future work. All proofs are in the appendix.

References:
[1] V. S. Borkar, J. Nair, and N. Sanketh, “Manufacturing consent,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control , vol. 60, no. 1, pp. 104–117, January 2015.
[2] S. Eshghi, V. Preciado, S. Sarkar, S. Venkatesh, Q. Zhao, R. D’Souza, and A. Swami, “Spread, then target, and advertise in waves: Optimal budget allocation across advertising channels,” IEEE Transactions on Network Science and Engineering , vol. 7, no. 2, pp. 750–763, October 2018.
[3] M. Goyal, D. Chatterjee, N. Karamchandani, and D. Manjunath, “Maintaining ferment,” in Proceedings of IEEE CDC , 2019, pp. 5217–5222.
[4] K. Palda, “ The measurement of cumulative advertising effects ,” The Journal of Business , vol. 38, pp. 162–179, 1965.
[5] D. Cowling, M. Modayil, and C. Stevens, “Assessing the relationship between ad volume and awareness of a tobacco education media campaign,” Tobacco Control , 2010. ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2976530/pdf/tc030692.pdf
[6] R. A. Holley and T. M. Liggett, “Ergodic theorems for weakly interacting infinite systems and the voter model,” Annals of Probability , vol. 3, no. 4, pp. 643–663, August 1975.
